title: The Hole Over Halley Bay
paragraphs: Most of Earth's ozone sits in a band of the stratosphere between roughly 15 and 35 kilometers up, and there is surprisingly little of it.
If every ozone molecule above a given spot were brought down to sea-level pressure and temperature, the layer would be about three millimeters thick.
That thickness is written as 300 Dobson units, after Gordon Dobson, the Oxford physicist whose instrument became the standard for measuring ozone in the 1920s, and it is close to the global average.
The layer matters because ozone absorbs most of the ultraviolet wavelengths that damage DNA and cause skin cancers and cataracts.
In 1930 the American engineer Thomas Midgley Jr. stood before a meeting of the American Chemical Society, inhaled a lungful of a new gas, and blew out a candle with it.
The gas was dichlorodifluoromethane, a chlorofluorocarbon, or CFC, developed at General Motors as a refrigerant.
The refrigerants of the day, ammonia, sulfur dioxide, and methyl chloride, were toxic, flammable, or both.

The new compounds were neither; stable, odorless, and cheap, they spread under the trade name Freon from refrigerators into air conditioners, aerosol spray cans, foam insulation, and solvents for cleaning electronics.
The first to look for CFCs in the open air was the British scientist James Lovelock, who had invented an extremely sensitive detector for such compounds.
In the early 1970s he carried it aboard a research ship bound for Antarctica and found CFC-11 in every sample, at only parts per trillion but present over the whole ocean.
Because nothing seemed to be removing the gas, Lovelock concluded that nearly all the CFCs ever released were still in the air, and he wrote that they posed no conceivable hazard.
It was not a careless remark; by every test then known, the gases were harmless.
Harmless at the surface is not harmless everywhere, and in 1974 Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland, at the University of California, Irvine, asked where the gases would finally go.
Their answer, published in Nature that June, was the stratosphere.
CFCs do not dissolve in rain and are not attacked by the reactive molecules that scrub most pollutants from the lower atmosphere, so they persist for decades and drift up past the ozone layer.
There they meet the hard ultraviolet light that ozone blocks for the rest of us, and it breaks the carbon-chlorine bond, releasing a free chlorine atom.
A chlorine atom pulls one oxygen atom from ozone, forming chlorine monoxide; chlorine monoxide then meets a free oxygen atom, hands over its oxygen, and the chlorine atom is back.
The chlorine is a catalyst, consumed by the first step and restored by the second, and one atom can repeat the cycle roughly a hundred thousand times before something else removes it.
Paul Crutzen had shown in 1970 that nitrogen oxides destroy ozone by a similar cycle, so the idea was not new, but the scale was.
The paper met resistance, and some of it was reasonable.
The manufacturers promised to stop production if a real threat were shown and argued that a calculation did not count.
Public opinion moved first: in 1978 the United States banned CFCs as propellants in most aerosol sprays, and Canada, Norway, and Sweden did the same.
Spray cans were only one use among several, however, and as refrigeration and foam production grew through the 1980s, total CFC output climbed back toward its peak.
The sign, when it came, came from the ground rather than from space.
The British Antarctic Survey had measured total ozone from Halley Bay, on the Brunt Ice Shelf, with a Dobson spectrophotometer since 1957.

Joseph Farman, Brian Gardiner, and Jonathan Shanklin noticed that the October readings, taken in the Antarctic spring, had been sliding since the late 1970s and by 1984 stood roughly a third below their earlier values.
Their report in Nature in May 1985 tied the loss to the growing burden of chlorine and suggested that something peculiar to the polar spring was at work.

An American satellite had measured ozone over Antarctica all along, but its software flagged values below a set threshold as probable error, and nobody examined the flagged data until the British paper appeared.
I find that sobering: the costliest instrument in the field had seen the hole and set it aside.
The finding fit the 1974 prediction in one way and contradicted it in others.

Chlorine was implicated, but Molina and Rowland had expected a slow, global loss of a few percent high in the stratosphere, not a collapse of a third lower down, confined to one continent and a few weeks each spring.

Within a year three explanations competed: a chemical one driven by chlorine, a dynamical one in which shifting winds lifted ozone-poor air from below, and a solar one blaming nitrogen oxides from a recent peak in solar activity.
The chemists had to admit that chlorine alone did not explain why the loss came only over the pole and only in spring.
The missing piece was ice.
In 1986 Susan Solomon of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration proposed, with Rowland and two colleagues, that the answer lay in polar stratospheric clouds.

Through the polar night a ring of winds called the polar vortex seals off the air above Antarctica, and without sunlight the stratosphere inside it cools below about minus 78 degrees Celsius, cold enough for thin clouds of nitric acid and water to form.
Elsewhere in the world most stratospheric chlorine is locked in two reservoir compounds, hydrogen chloride and chlorine nitrate, that do not attack ozone.
On the cloud particles, however, the reservoirs react with each other and release molecular chlorine, while the nitric acid stays in the particles, which can grow heavy enough to fall away.

When the sun returns in September it splits the chlorine molecules into atoms, and because free oxygen atoms are scarce at those altitudes the destruction runs by a second route, in which two chlorine monoxide molecules pair up and are split by sunlight.
Ozone over the continent falls by half or more within a few weeks.
The hypothesis was tested quickly.
That same spring Solomon led a ground expedition to McMurdo Station that measured unusually high levels of chlorine oxides.

The following year a high-altitude ER-2 aircraft flew from Punta Arenas, Chile, into the vortex, and its instruments showed chlorine monoxide climbing sharply exactly where ozone fell, a mirror image as close to a smoking gun as atmospheric science usually gets.
The dynamical and solar explanations faded; neither could account for the chlorine.
Diplomacy did not wait for the aircraft.
The Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer was signed in September 1987 and took effect at the start of 1989.
Its original terms were modest: a freeze in production of the main CFCs, then a cut of 50 percent by 1999.

A clause required the parties to revisit the targets as the science changed, and amendments adopted in London in 1990 and Copenhagen in 1992 turned the half measure into a halt: production in developed countries ended in 1996, and developing countries, given more time and a fund for substitutes, followed by 2010.

The treaty has since been ratified by every member state of the United Nations, and a 2016 amendment adopted in Kigali, Rwanda, extended it to hydrofluorocarbons, substitutes that spare ozone but trap heat powerfully.

It is fashionable to call Montreal the most successful environmental treaty ever written, and I think the praise is earned, with one reservation: the problem was comparatively easy, since substitutes existed and the manufacturers were few.
In 1995 Crutzen, Molina, and Rowland shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Stratospheric chlorine peaked in the late 1990s and has fallen slowly since, because the gases that carry it live for decades to a century.
In 2016 Solomon and her colleagues reported the first firm evidence that the September hole was shrinking, and current assessments expect Antarctic ozone to recover to its 1980 state in the 2060s.
The lag is the lesson I would draw from the whole affair.
Because CFCs are so stable, the atmosphere answers a decision only slowly: the hole was found a decade after the warning and will close a lifetime after the ban.

questions.stem: According to the passage, 300 Dobson units corresponds to
choices: the altitude at which stratospheric ozone is most concentrated
ozone about three millimeters thick at sea-level conditions
the fraction of harmful ultraviolet light the layer absorbs
the thickness of the stratospheric band that holds the ozone
the amount of ozone lost over Antarctica in a typical spring

proof.quote: the layer would be about three millimeters thick
That thickness is written as 300 Dobson units

questions.why: Paragraph 1 says that if all the ozone above a spot were brought down to sea-level pressure and temperature the layer would be about three millimeters thick, and the next sentence names that thickness 300 Dobson units.
distractorNotes: Wrong quantity: paragraph 1 gives 15 to 35 kilometers as where the ozone sits, not what a Dobson unit measures.
Outside the passage: the unit measures the amount of ozone, not the light it absorbs.
Wrong quantity: the band is 15 to 35 kilometers deep; the Dobson unit describes the ozone squeezed to sea-level conditions.
Wrong paragraph: the spring loss belongs to paragraph 6 and is not what the unit defines.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the CFCs developed at General Motors replaced earlier refrigerants that
choices: were too expensive to produce in large quantities
left an unpleasant odor that lingered in kitchens
broke down quickly inside sealed machinery
were poisonous, flammable, or sometimes both
could not be adapted for use in air conditioners

proof.quote: were toxic, flammable, or both

questions.why: Paragraph 2 names the refrigerants of the day, ammonia, sulfur dioxide, and methyl chloride, and says they were toxic, flammable, or both; the new compounds were neither.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: cheapness is listed as a virtue of the new compounds, not as a fault of the old.
Reversed: odorless is a virtue of the new gas; nothing says the old ones smelled.
Outside the passage: stability is credited to the new compounds, but the old ones are never said to break down.
Outside the passage: air conditioners are a place the new compounds spread to, not a failing of the old ones.

questions.stem: The author's comment in paragraph 3 that Lovelock's judgment 'was not a careless remark' serves primarily to
choices: show that the danger was invisible to the tests of the time
criticize Lovelock for ignoring the warning of Molina and Rowland
argue that his detector was too crude to measure CFCs reliably
support the manufacturers' later claim that no threat had been demonstrated
suggest that CFCs are in fact harmless to the ozone layer

proof.quote: by every test then known, the gases were harmless

questions.why: Paragraph 3 follows the remark with its reason: by every test then known, the gases were harmless. The author is explaining how a careful scientist could reach the wrong conclusion, not blaming him.
distractorNotes: Anachronism: Molina and Rowland's warning in paragraph 4 came after Lovelock wrote, so he could not have ignored it.
Reversed: paragraph 3 calls his detector extremely sensitive.
Wrong paragraph: the manufacturers' argument belongs to paragraph 5, and the author does not use Lovelock to support it.
Contradicted: paragraph 4 opens by saying harmless at the surface is not harmless everywhere.

questions.stem: According to the passage, after a chlorine atom takes an oxygen atom from ozone, the resulting chlorine monoxide
choices: dissolves in rain and is washed out of the stratosphere
absorbs hard ultraviolet light and splits into chlorine and oxygen
combines with nitrogen oxides to form a stable compound
reacts with a second ozone molecule to rebuild the ozone it destroyed
hands its oxygen to a free oxygen atom and frees the chlorine

proof.quote: chlorine monoxide then meets a free oxygen atom, hands over its oxygen, and the chlorine atom is back

questions.why: Paragraph 4 lays out both steps: the chlorine atom takes an oxygen from ozone to form chlorine monoxide, and chlorine monoxide then meets a free oxygen atom, hands over its oxygen, and the chlorine atom is back.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 4 says CFCs do not dissolve in rain, and nothing is washed out of the stratosphere.
Wrong paragraph: sunlight splitting a chlorine compound appears in paragraph 8, and there it is molecular chlorine, not chlorine monoxide.
Outside the passage: paragraph 8 names chlorine nitrate as a reservoir but never says chlorine monoxide forms it in this cycle.
Reversed: the cycle destroys ozone; nothing in it rebuilds ozone.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if CFCs dissolved readily in rainwater, they would most likely
choices: release their chlorine atoms more quickly in the lower atmosphere
form polar stratospheric clouds at much warmer temperatures
be removed from the air before reaching the ozone layer
destroy ozone through a different catalytic cycle
persist in the atmosphere for even longer than they do now

proof.quote: CFCs do not dissolve in rain and are not attacked by the reactive molecules that scrub most pollutants from the lower atmosphere, so they persist for decades and drift up past the ozone layer

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says CFCs persist and drift up past the ozone layer because they do not dissolve in rain and are not scrubbed out like most pollutants. Take away that resistance and rain would remove them before they climbed.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: chlorine is freed only by hard ultraviolet light in the stratosphere, and rain is never said to release it.
Unrelated: the clouds in paragraph 8 form from nitric acid and water, not from CFCs.
Outside the passage: no alternative cycle for dissolved CFCs is described.
Reversed: being washed out is the opposite of persisting.

questions.stem: All of the following are mentioned in the passage as uses of CFCs EXCEPT:
choices: fire extinguishers
refrigerators
aerosol spray cans
foam insulation
solvents for cleaning electronics

proof.quote: refrigerators
aerosol spray cans
foam insulation
solvents for cleaning electronics

questions.why: Paragraph 2 lists refrigerators, air conditioners, aerosol spray cans, foam insulation, and solvents for cleaning electronics. Fire extinguishers never appear anywhere in the passage.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 2 says the compounds spread from refrigerators into their other uses.
Paragraph 2 lists aerosol spray cans, and paragraph 5 returns to them.
Paragraph 2 lists foam insulation.
Paragraph 2 lists solvents for cleaning electronics.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the measurements that first revealed the Antarctic ozone loss were made
choices: by an American satellite launched in 1957
from a high-altitude aircraft flying out of Chile
at McMurdo Station during the Antarctic spring of 1986
from a ground station on the Brunt Ice Shelf
aboard a research ship bound for Antarctica

proof.quote: measured total ozone from Halley Bay, on the Brunt Ice Shelf, with a Dobson spectrophotometer since 1957
came from the ground rather than from space

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says the sign came from the ground rather than from space: the British Antarctic Survey had measured total ozone from Halley Bay, on the Brunt Ice Shelf, since 1957.
distractorNotes: Mash-up: 1957 is when the ground record began, and paragraph 6 says the satellite data were set aside, not that they revealed the loss.
Wrong paragraph: the aircraft flights in paragraph 9 confirmed the chlorine two years after the loss was reported.
Wrong paragraph: the McMurdo expedition in paragraph 9 came a year after the report.
Wrong paragraph: the ship in paragraph 3 carried Lovelock's detector for CFCs, not ozone.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the satellite failed to reveal the ozone loss because
choices: its sensor could not detect ozone values below a certain minimum level
its data-handling rules set aside the very readings that mattered
it was launched too late to record the decline that began in the late 1970s
it measured ozone only in the upper stratosphere
its orbit did not carry it over Antarctica in October

proof.quote: its software flagged values below a set threshold as probable error, and nobody examined the flagged data
had seen the hole and set it aside

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says the satellite had measured ozone all along; what failed was the rule that flagged low values as probable error and the fact that nobody examined the flagged data. The author sums it up: the instrument had seen the hole and set it aside.
distractorNotes: Half right: the readings were low, but the sensor recorded them; it was the software that flagged them as suspect.
Contradicted: paragraph 6 says the satellite had measured ozone over Antarctica all along.
Outside the passage: nothing limits the satellite to the upper stratosphere.
Contradicted: the satellite measured over Antarctica; the problem was what happened to the readings afterward.

questions.stem: The author presents three competing explanations in paragraph 7 primarily to
choices: argue that shifting winds were the most plausible explanation for the loss
show that Molina and Rowland had been mistaken about the role of chlorine
suggest that the solar cycle had been overlooked by chemists
introduce the satellite data that would settle the dispute
show that chlorine alone did not yet explain the pattern of the loss

proof.quote: chlorine alone did not explain why the loss came only over the pole and only in spring
contradicted it in others

questions.why: Paragraph 7 opens by saying the finding contradicted the 1974 prediction in several ways and closes by admitting that chlorine alone did not explain why the loss came only over the pole and only in spring. The three explanations show the question was still open.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 9 says the dynamical explanation faded, and the author never favors it.
Too strong: paragraph 7 says chlorine was implicated, as predicted; the prediction was incomplete, not wrong.
Outside the passage: the solar idea is listed as one competitor, not as something chemists overlooked.
Wrong paragraph and reversed: satellite data appear in paragraph 6, and the dispute was settled by aircraft in paragraph 9.

questions.stem: According to the passage, polar stratospheric clouds form over Antarctica because
choices: chlorine nitrate condenses as soon as it meets hydrogen chloride
the returning spring sunlight lifts moisture into the stratosphere
nitric acid falling from the particles seeds new clouds below
winds carry ozone-poor air upward from the lower atmosphere
sealed-off air cools far below freezing during the polar night

proof.quote: the polar vortex seals off the air above Antarctica, and without sunlight the stratosphere inside it cools below about minus 78 degrees Celsius, cold enough for thin clouds of nitric acid and water to form

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says the polar vortex seals off the air above Antarctica, and without sunlight the stratosphere inside it cools below about minus 78 degrees Celsius, cold enough for the clouds to form.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 8 says the reservoirs react on the cloud particles; they do not make the clouds.
Reversed: the clouds form during the sunless winter, and the spring sun is what activates the chlorine.
Reversed: paragraph 8 says the nitric acid stays in the particles and can fall away; it does not seed clouds.
Wrong paragraph: rising ozone-poor air is the dynamical hypothesis from paragraph 7, which paragraph 9 says faded.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 8, the word 'reservoir' most nearly means
choices: a form in which something is held out of use
an artificial lake that stores water for a city
an extra supply kept back for use in emergencies
a container that collects runoff
a source that steadily releases its contents

proof.quote: two reservoir compounds, hydrogen chloride and chlorine nitrate, that do not attack ozone

questions.why: Paragraph 8 calls hydrogen chloride and chlorine nitrate reservoir compounds that do not attack ozone: the chlorine is held in them, inactive, until the cloud particles release it.
distractorNotes: This is the everyday meaning of the word, but no water or lake is involved in the sentence.
Close but off: the chlorine is not being saved for later use; it is locked up and inactive.
Nothing in the sentence collects anything; the compounds hold chlorine chemically.
Reversed: the reservoirs hold chlorine and do not attack ozone; release happens only on the cloud particles.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the 1987 aircraft flights into the polar vortex showed that
choices: ozone-poor air was being lifted from the lower atmosphere
chlorine monoxide rose sharply where ozone dropped
nitrogen oxides had built up after the peak in solar activity
polar stratospheric clouds were made of nitric acid and water
the ozone loss extended well beyond the edge of the vortex

proof.quote: its instruments showed chlorine monoxide climbing sharply exactly where ozone fell

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says the ER-2's instruments showed chlorine monoxide climbing sharply exactly where ozone fell, a mirror image the author calls a smoking gun.
distractorNotes: Reversed: that is the dynamical hypothesis, which paragraph 9 says faded after the flights.
Reversed: that is the solar hypothesis, which also faded; the flights measured chlorine, not nitrogen oxides.
Wrong paragraph: the makeup of the clouds is given in paragraph 8 as part of Solomon's proposal, not as an aircraft result.
Outside the passage: nothing is said about ozone beyond the vortex.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the Montreal Protocol is best described as
choices: entirely dismissive
unreservedly enthusiastic
approving but qualified
studiously neutral
deeply anxious

proof.quote: I think the praise is earned, with one reservation

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says plainly that the praise for Montreal is earned, then adds one reservation: the problem was comparatively easy. That is approval with a qualification attached.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the author calls the praise earned.
Too strong: the author attaches a reservation to the praise.
Too weak: the author takes a clear position in the first person.
Wrong register: nothing in paragraph 10 expresses worry about the treaty.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following is true of the Montreal Protocol EXCEPT:
choices: It took effect at the beginning of 1989.
Its original terms called for a 50 percent cut by 1999.
Every member state of the United Nations has ratified it.
Its original terms halted all CFC production at once.
An amendment adopted in 2016 extended it to hydrofluorocarbons.

proof.quote: took effect at the start of 1989
then a cut of 50 percent by 1999
ratified by every member state of the United Nations
a 2016 amendment adopted in Kigali, Rwanda, extended it to hydrofluorocarbons
Its original terms were modest: a freeze in production of the main CFCs

questions.why: Paragraph 10 calls the original terms modest: a freeze, then a 50 percent cut by 1999. The full halt came only with the London and Copenhagen amendments, and even then production in developed countries ran until 1996.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 10 says the treaty took effect at the start of 1989.
Paragraph 10 gives the original target as a cut of 50 percent by 1999.
Paragraph 10 says every member state of the United Nations has ratified it.
Paragraph 10 describes the 2016 Kigali amendment covering hydrofluorocarbons.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the ozone hole kept appearing each spring for years after CFC production ended in developed countries because
choices: the polar vortex grew stronger each winter after the ban
hydrofluorocarbons released as substitutes destroy ozone as well
the CFCs already released remained in the atmosphere for decades
the Montreal Protocol did not take effect until 2010
polar stratospheric clouds persist for decades once they have formed

proof.quote: because the gases that carry it live for decades to a century
Because CFCs are so stable, the atmosphere answers a decision only slowly
they persist for decades

questions.why: Paragraph 11 says stratospheric chlorine has fallen only slowly because the gases that carry it live for decades to a century, and that the atmosphere answers a decision only slowly because CFCs are so stable. The gas released before the ban was still up there.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: nothing is said about the vortex changing from year to year.
Contradicted: paragraph 10 says hydrofluorocarbons spare ozone.
Wrong date: paragraph 10 says the treaty took effect in 1989; 2010 was the developing countries' deadline.
Outside the passage: the clouds form each polar night in paragraph 8; nothing says they last for decades.

questions.stem: Which new situation best illustrates the principle described in paragraph 11?
choices: A city bans a pesticide that breaks down within days, and its river is clean by the following summer.
A town stops burying a chemical that lasts for centuries, and its wells stay tainted for decades.
A factory switches to a cleaner fuel on Monday, and the haze over the town is gone by Friday.
A village plants trees on a bare slope, and the first storm washes the seedlings away.
A farmer stops applying fertilizer, and the very next harvest is noticeably smaller than the last.

proof.quote: Because CFCs are so stable, the atmosphere answers a decision only slowly
the gases that carry it live for decades to a century

questions.why: Paragraph 11's principle is that when a pollutant is very stable, stopping its release pays off only slowly, because what was already released lingers. Wells that stay tainted for decades after the burials stop follow the same rule.
distractorNotes: Reversed: a pollutant that breaks down within days brings a fast recovery, the opposite of the lag.
Reversed: the haze clears within days, so there is no lag.
Wrong mechanism: the seedlings are lost to a storm, not to a lingering pollutant.
Wrong direction: this is an immediate cost of stopping, not a delayed benefit.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: The discovery of the Antarctic ozone hole proved that satellites are less reliable than ground-based instruments for monitoring the atmosphere
Thomas Midgley's refrigerants caused more environmental damage than any other invention of the twentieth century
The Montreal Protocol succeeded only because the chemical industry had already developed cheap substitutes for the CFCs it gave up
A chemical threat predicted on paper was confirmed by a surprise Antarctic discovery and answered by a treaty whose effects unfold slowly
Polar stratospheric clouds, not CFCs, are the true cause of the seasonal ozone loss over Antarctica

proof.quote: asked where the gases would finally go
The sign, when it came, came from the ground rather than from space.
The lag is the lesson I would draw from the whole affair.

questions.why: The passage moves from a prediction on paper in 1974, through the unexpected Antarctic discovery and the chemistry that explained it, to a treaty and a recovery that will take decades. Only the answer carries all three parts.
distractorNotes: Too narrow: the satellite story is one sobering detail in paragraph 6, not the point of the passage.
Too narrow and outside the passage: Midgley appears only in paragraph 2, and the author never ranks his invention against others.
Too strong: the author calls substitutes one reason the problem was easier, not the only reason the treaty succeeded.
Reversed: paragraph 8 says the clouds activate chlorine that came from CFCs; they are the mechanism, not a rival cause.
